en: K4 Checked (98.8) Vādhūlaśrautasūtra 9, Vājapeya. (M)p.311-, (T)p.637- <9.1.1>p[K4,66a7-;M311-312]
Now follows the Vājapeya sacrifice.

One who is about to perform the Vājapeya collects the necessary materials: seventeen hundred cattle, seventeen birds of each species, seventeen men, seventeen elephants, seventeen yoked chariots, a wooden vessel made of Udumbara wood with seventeen spokes and ten wheels, seventeen gold neck-ornaments (niṣkas), seventeen pieces of gold, seventeen kinds of herbs, and seventeen varieties of wild rice (nīvāra).

Seventeen vessels, seventeen drums, seventeen *vāyavya* cups, seventeen *upayāma* cups, seventeen dark-colored, uniform goats dedicated to Prajāpati, seventeen garments, a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) measuring seventeen *aratnis*, seventeen *pravyādha* targets at the distance of an arrow-shot; then the others: seventeen [items], and here the others consist of a bundle of wheat, a ten-step path, a resting place, a goat-skin, a black antelope skin, a *śamāna* (?), a stool, and a gold weight of one hundred *mānas*.

A garment of fine silk, a turban, a *vāra* cloth, and a *sata* cloth; animals dedicated to various deities; five cups for Indra; the cup for the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice; a golden vessel; and two mongooses facing each other—these are his ritual materials that have been prepared.

The deliberation concerning the consecration (*dīkṣā*): there are thirteen consecrations, three *upasads*, and the pressing on the seventeenth day; thus say others, "This sacrificial rite belongs to Prajāpati.
However, there are indeed seventeen consecrations, three *upasads*, and the pressing on the twenty-first day.
By means of the consecrations they thus bring Prajāpati together, and by means of the twenty-first [day] they establish Āditya. He undergoes the consecration with the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* [offering].

Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he offers the *sāvitra* oblation into the *āhavanīya* fire with four ladlings, reciting: "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice," and "To Bhaga... svadhā-tine svāhā!"

One should release speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) for the *Prāyaṇīya* offering; at the call to the preparer of the oblation for the *Ātithya*; after three of the *Upasads*; before the three calls of the *Saṃpraiṣa*; before the carrying forward of the fire; before the *Vaisarjana* rite; before the bringing near of the animal victim; after the three offerings of the drops (*vipruṣ*) of the three pressings; and before the three rising ceremonies.

Before the *ṣoḍaśin* chant of the *saṃpraiṣa*, and before the *bṛhat* chant, the *agni* offerings are made. Before the *bṛhat* chant, the *agni* offerings are made. During the three-day period preceding the day of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), they prepare the *surā*; this [surā] is completed together with the day of the pressing.

He offers the oblations of the *devasū* together with the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the one dedicated to Agni and Soma. These eight [oblations] begin with "To Agni, the lord of the house. The animal-cake is accompanied by the formal calls (*praiṣa*). [The calls are: "Recite for the [deities]... for the *sviṣṭakṛt*... for Viṣṇu... for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he says to him: "May Savitṛ impel you among those who impel," and "Agni is the lord of the lords of the household."

With the verse, “O gods who are among the gods, dwelling in well-being,” he takes his right hand, saying, “May he be the king of the Brāhmaṇas, the son of such-and-such and the grandson of such-and-such.

Then follow the Viṣṇu-strides with the formulas, “Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu; thou art the wide-strider. Then the morning libations are offered together with the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*); the oblation for Bṛhaspati (*bārhaspatya-caru*) is cooked.
With that same [filter], seventeen bowls of milk are prepared.

At the time when the Adhvaryu goes toward the water, at that very time the Pratiprasthātṛ, [using the formula] "O Purifier, [purify] the fermented liquor," pours the *surā* into a vessel behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart through the filter, [with the verse]: "Soma’s daughter has purified Soma with the eternal filter."
Having arrived and sipped water, they consecrate the king;
the cups (grahas) are drawn in the established manner.

Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa from the Āgrayaṇa vessel, he draws the *atigrāhya* cups with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; thee, the bull, seated on the wood, seated in the world, I draw as one pleasing to Indra. This is thy womb; for Indra thee! Thou art taken with a support; thee, seated in the waters, I draw... for Indra thee! Thou art taken with a support; thee, seated on the earth, I draw..."

"This for Indra—this for you, O Indra! I take the draughts belonging to the five peoples, the highest one. This is your womb; for Indra, you!"—saying this, while they both move across, the Pratiprasthātṛ creeps along behind the axle.
The Adhvaryu takes up seventeen vessels dedicated to Vāyu.
When seventeen [cups] have been taken, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes seven *upayāma* vessels; the Adhvaryu takes the Soma cups, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the Surā cups.
The Adhvaryu places the Soma cups to the east of the axle.

Subsequently, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the cups of *surā* with the verse, "With this foundation, engendering deeds" (1.7.12.2g-f). With one [verse], "For he, the glowing one, has sent forth his wide body; thou art taken with a base; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati," the Adhvaryu takes the Soma cups.
He sets them down without touching the previous ladle, saying, "This is thy womb; for Prajāpati, thee."

With the verse, "O friend, indeed, O friend" (1.8.21.1d + 1.7.12.2g), the Pratiprasthātṛ takes one draught of *surā* with the formula: "They have come like those possessing barley; thou art taken with a base (*upayāma*); I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati. This is thy womb; for Prajāpati thee. Or alternatively, he deposits it with the words, "For Bṛhaspati.
In this manner, the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ take these draughts respectively, seventeen at a time.
Having touched water, the Pratiprasthātṛ hastens forward.

With the verse, "The winds flow honey for the one who acts according to the Ṛta" (4.2.9.3g + 1.7.12.2g), the Adhvaryu takes the honey-draught with a golden vessel: "The rivers flow honey; the plants [flow honey]. You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to the waters and to the plants. This is your womb: to the waters and to the plants. He deposits it and takes the Ukthya draught; he takes the Dhruva draught.
The ritual act is accomplished through the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

He encircles the post with six ropes and hides six *svaru*-chips. Then, with the formula "For food, thee! (*iṣe tvā*), having placed forty-four blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and having offered the introductory oblation (*upākaraṇīya*), he dedicates the animals: a goat for Agni, a goat for Indra-Agni, a goat for Indra, a ewe for Sarasvatī, and a spotted heifer for the Maruts.
At the *adhyṛṣabha* rite, these two [cows] should be without calves;
having brought forward seventeen dark-colored, uniform goats for Prajāpati, he proceeds with the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*).
Then, taking twenty-two cords with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he fastens them to the animals.
He yokes the animals dedicated to various deities in successive order, and those dedicated to Prajāpati as he desires;

having sprinkled the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, he makes them drink water in successive order, and those dedicated to various deities as he desires; having set down the animals dedicated to Prajāpati after sprinkling them, and having repeatedly set down the vessels after sprinkling them, he recites the invitatory verse for Agni as he is being kindled.
When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, having poured the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon, he says: "O *Āgnīdh*, cleanse the fires three times each!

Having stepped across without touching the northern ladle (*sruc*) with the other, he anoints the animals in order, one after another, according to their respective deities, as many as there are, including those for Prajāpati. Having anointed the *dhruvā* ladle and set it down, he proceeds with the *pravara*.
Having produced the two *sruva*-ladles, he takes them up.

He says, "O descendant of Prajāpati, cause [the announcement] to be heard! He performs the *prayāja* offerings. He says, "O Śrauṣaṭ! Cause [the announcement] to be heard! He says, "Prompt for the *samidh*s! [And then] "Prompt! Prompt!"
He performs eleven after-offerings (*anuyāja*).
He pours everything from the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *sruk* at the fourth and eighth offerings, leaving the eleventh remaining; having performed ten, he steps across.

With the verse, "Those with axes in their hands," he proceeds separately for the various deities and the *prājāpatya* offerings. Having covered the *svaru* chips and placed the two ladles (*srucau*) in their respective places, he says, "Recite for the fire that has been carried around" (*paryagnaye 'nubrūhi*). With a firebrand in his hand, he runs around [the altar]; he offers the five *apāvya* formulas.

The Hotṛ offers the sixth oblation. The Adhvaryu [takes] the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the purpose of making the response. The Pratiprasthātṛ [takes] forty animals; they touch those animals from behind. The Pratiprasthātṛ [takes] forty [animals]; they touch those animals from behind.
With the mantra, "Protect [them], being in contact with the earth; protect [them] from the *pānna*," he scatters twenty-two blades of *barhis* grass.
Upon these, they place the animals.
A goat for Agni, a goat for Indra-Agni, a goat for Indra, a ewe for Sarasvatī, a speckled heifer for the Maruts, and a six-year-old cow for Prajāpati—of these they bring the omenta.
Having carried them across between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ, turning toward the north from the south, roasts the omenta.
From those two, the Adhvaryu throws down twenty-two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the verse, "Thee, O Agni, they have established as the bearer of oblations.
Having made the one for Agni the last, he makes an offering with the *sruva* ladle; [the drops] fall toward the hundredfold [oblation].
Those droplets fall upon them.

"Recite for the small portions," he says. Having sprinkled the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) and having made the offering to Agni the last one, he makes an oblation with the dipping-spoon (sruva). The others [portions] are held back;
they fall as droplets, and the droplets fly upward.

"Recite for the small portions," he says; then, having brought the clarified butter and a piece of gold, he spreads the clarified butter and the piece of gold beneath the omentum. They proceed with the offerings for various deities separately.

He proceeds with the omenta of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati as if with a single one. Having performed the offering of the omenta of those dedicated to Prajāpati, they purify themselves with the three verses beginning, "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss."
They proceed to the *cātvāla* pit;
thus the rite is accomplished. Together with the morning-offering cakes (*prātassavanīya-puroḍāśa*), he places the *caru* for Bṛhaspati.

Having offered the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) of the morning pressing, he says, "Recite for Bṛhaspati! As the Hotṛ places the portion of the cake for Bṛhaspati—which has been spread with butter and sprinkled over—he himself recites the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for it. He says, "The Hotṛ sacrifices; O, cause [the Āgnīdhra] to announce! and then, "Sacrifice to Bṛhaspati!"
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers;

having offered this oblation to Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt—which has not yet had its *sviṣṭakṛt* performed—they carry it back to the Āgnīdhra. Having run to the *śūlāmārutyā*, he says, "I shall cook the items that are not to be discarded," and thus the morning pressing is successfully completed.
The midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) is accomplished up to the *pavamāna* chant.

Having performed the rite with the *pavamāna*, he issues the command: "O *Āgnīdh*, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); prepare the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*); O Pratiprasthātṛ, bring the curds for the Sovereign (*samrāj*); O Hotṛ, speak what you have to say.
Having thus acted regarding the curds for the Sovereign, he proceeds by moving forward.

Following that direction, he offers two oblations for the Hotṛ; those which they consume while reciting at the Pavamāna, and those Nārāśaṃsa cups which he recites over, and those portions of the omentum of the barren cow—with these having been offered, he sets aside the portions to be cut off for the Soma-cups.
Without cutting off the portions, he sets aside the spit-entrails for the Surā-cups. He proceeds with the Mādhyandina sacrificial cakes.
Of these, he offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation for the one dedicated to Bṛhaspati; the *sviṣṭakṛt* is offered,
the common *iḍā* is established, and the ritual action is completed when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups are set down.
The Nārāśaṃsa cups sink down when the Nārāśaṃsas have been set down;
the sacrificer puts on a garment of *tārpya* wool, and he wraps around himself a turban made of darbha grass with the formula: "Thou art the womb of sovereignty."
At this time, they cause the wife to put on [the garment]. He brings down the chariot with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; through thee may he slay Vṛtra.
He turns it toward the west from the east with the verse, "Now at the impulse of strength, the great mother... and with the words, "We invoke by name that Diti in whom this [world] was produced."
They place it to the south of the *sadas* and to the south of the *sadas*-hall on the southern path, facing east.
He washes three horses with the formula: "The nectar is within the waters; the medicine is within the waters," and [with] "O swift ones, you are the nectar of the waters."

7. With the words, “Either Vāyu shall yoke thee, or Manu shall yoke thee,” he yokes the chariot drawn by side-horses (*praṣṭivāhin*). There should be a side-horse on the north; with the verse, “The Gandharvas have bestowed the sevenfold speed,” and 8. with the verse, “O grandson of the Waters, swift-coursing one,” he strokes them. With the verse, “May the wave that wins the prize...,” and “After this let the chariots be yoked,” he speaks.

Following that, the chariots are yoked to the east of the sacrificial post on the racecourse; there are sixteen of them, and this one is their seventeenth. Along the northern edge of the altar, seventeen drums are beaten.
At the edge of the *catvāla* pit, at the height of the navel, they fix chariot wheels.
To the north of the *āgnīdhra* shed, he yokes a horse harnessed by the side, with the formula: "With the yoking of the sacrifice."

Having gone around the Āgnīdhra fire-altar by the north, he offers the Dakṣiṇā oblations after having led the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) to the south. Approaching the chariot with the Viṣṇu-strides, saying, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he touches its two wheels on both sides of the chariot while reciting, "Thou art the step of Viṣṇu, thou art the wide stride of Viṣṇu; the two hooks, the two downward-hooks—may they carry us across."
11. Having paid homage with the words, "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he mounts the chariot with the words, "Through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize, may I win the prize. 12.
With the words, "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ," the Brahman ascends the chariot wheel with the words, "Through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize, may I ascend the highest firmament (nāka)."

13. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," [saying this] the Adhvaryu makes the Brahman or the sacrificer recite while looking at him: "May I ascend the highest firmament by means of Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize, through the sacred word (brahman).
14. "The horse-whip," [saying this] he takes up the horse-whip: "O spirited one, win the prize!"

15. With the words, “*Arvāsi*,” he urges on the horses. [With the words,] “*Hayo ’asi*... [15] ... he stands upon the drums. 16. He says to him, “*Indrāya vācaṃ vadata*” (1.7.8.1c), and [he says], “*Indraṃ vājaṃ vājam ajayat*” (K4, M:
*ajayid*). In this very manner, having gone forth while striking them until the very end, the chariot returns.

17. "May Agni win speech with the one-syllable [word]," saying this, he gives seventeen pieces of gold to the race-winners (*ājisṛt*), using these [formulas]: "May they win! May they win! and "May they conquer! May they conquer!"

With the verse, "O swift horses, winners of the prize" (1.7.8.3), he causes these three horses—the steeds of Bṛhaspati—to smell the *caru* offering dedicated to Bṛhaspati, saying: "About to run for the prize, about to win the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati!
With the formula, "Thou art a steed," he anoints the ear of the horse that is being harnessed to the right, saying: "Thou art a courser, thou art a racer, thou art a swift steed."
Thus [it is said].
<9.6>/<9.3.1> He issues the command: "O racers, run in the race! and "O drum-beater, strike the drums! O Brahman, sing the *vājina-sāman* for the racers!"

They perform this: those who have entered the race run on the race-course; those who strike the drums beat the drums; while being encircled by the chariot wheels, the Brahman priest sings the *Sāman* of the *vājins*.

21 He consecrates them with the mantra, "O *vājins*, run for the prize (*vāja*)," and with, "Go forth, go forth, to the Maruts! 22 He causes them to reach the goal with the verse, "In every contest, O *vājins*, protect us," and he makes them turn back with the four verses beginning, "Among the riches, O sages... and ending, "...the serpent-like one."

23. "And indeed, of him as he runs, as he hastens..."—with this [verse], one should offer an *avacchinna-homa* (a sacrifice for what has been interrupted) into the Āhavanīya fire if the running [of the chariot] should be interrupted.
24. "And indeed, of him as he runs..."—if [the running] is interrupted while they are running; "May the leaves carry us across anew, svāhā!"—[this is the verse]. 25.
"May the impulse of strength come to me..."—with this [verse], one offers the *rathavimocanīyā* (chariot-unyoking) oblations, [concluding with]: "...may it come to Heaven and Earth, svāhā!"—thus.

When this [oblation] has been offered, they unyoke the chariots with the verses beginning, "O swift steeds, winners of the prize. Having taken portions from these very three horses and from the oblation for Bṛhaspati, he wipes them on the right sides of their axles with the words, "Win the prize—wipe yourselves.
With the words, "This was that true compact of yours," he unyokes the drums with the verse, "That which by Indra... unyoke the prize."
The race-winners (*ājisṛt*) bring him pieces of gold.

While they are being brought, he offers seventeen spoonfuls (*sruva-āhuti*) with the formula: "Agni won speech by means of the one-syllable [meter]," "They two have won," and "They have won. Whatever remains there in the vessel, having made it a cup for Sura, he hands it over to the race-winners.

With these words—"I purchase you with that by which you won the prize"—and with these chips of gold and the honey-cup, the sacrificer approaches the Brahman priest who has descended at the edge of the *cātvāla* pit: "With mind I consume you; with speech I consume you; with breath, sight, and hearing I consume you; [for the sake of] life. Then the Brahman priest consumes it: "With mind I consume you; with speech I consume you; with breath, sight, and hearing I consume you; for life."
And he gives this gold and the horse-chariot to the Brahman priest; he assigns the other chariots to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
for the sacrificer alone there are pieces of gold.

Just as the priests go toward the northern shoulder of the altar with the royal purchases, so do the race-horse runners go toward the southern hip. Having arrived and touched water, they cause the Soma-cups and the portions to be cut;
having caused them to be cut, he places them for the priests, saying: "You are united; may you unite me with prosperity."

The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) come bringing the *surā*-cups and the portions not to be offered, saying, "You are separators; separate me from evil. Neither of them consume [the portions], for they cause a dispersal among the race-runners (*ājisṛt*). With that [portion], they should consume the *surā*-cups, [reciting]: "Manu generated the gods here; Manu [generated] this entire world; Manu became the light here, the ascetic dwelling upon the earth."
"If they do not eat [the portions], they should pour [the remnants] around the *mārjālīya* fire in this very manner"; thus indeed they pour [the remnants] around the *mārjālīya*.

He says, "Sing of the living King!"—they should sing of Manu himself. Having arrived, he offers the twelve *vājaprasavīya* oblations with the formula, "To strength, svāhā!"... (4)... he says, "To progeny, to the overlord, svāhā! and "To offspring, to the overlord, svāhā! He mixes all the herbs with curds.

With the verse, “The impulse of strength has brought forth this one at the beginning” (1.7.10.1a), he offers seven oblations of food with a ladle made of Udumbara wood; with the words, “King Soma,” he offers the seventh with a *pātrī* vessel; he pours out [the remainder] with the ladle for the sake of the consecration, saying, “To Varuṇa... svāhā. He offers six *pārtha* oblations; [this is] the sacrifice consisting of six elements.
To the east of the two *havirdhāna* sheds and to the west of the *āhavanīya* fire, he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and its hairy side upward;
upon it, the sacrificer sits, turned toward the east and drawing his knees up into his lap.

With the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he sprinkles him with the *sruva* ladle made of *udumbara* wood; with those two [formulas], "I sprinkle thee with Sarasvatī... and "...I sprinkle thee," says the Brāhmaṇa. With the formula, "I sprinkle thee with the sovereignty of Indra," he sprinkles a *rājanya*; with the formula, "I sprinkle thee with the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati," he sprinkles a king (*rājan*).
He sprinkles him with the entire [substance] together, letting it flow down as far as his mouth. He offers exactly six *pārtha* oblations.
The sacrificial post is wrapped with seventeen cloths;
it is hornless, four-cornered, and has a flour-cake top-ring (*caṣāla*) turned downward.
As they lead the wives forward, the sacrificer says to her: "Come, O wife! Let us two ascend to heaven."

"Indeed, let him ascend to heaven," she said—[with the words] "May life be perfected through the sacrifice," and so on with the ten *kalpa* formulas... "may he ascend. The *pratiprasthātṛ* should cause him to ascend with these [formulas], beginning with "May breath through the sacrifice... may the sacrifice be perfected through the sacrifice."
33. With the verse, “The swan dwelling in the pure [heaven],” he measures the navel on the top-ring.

With the verse, “The Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the great,” 34. he makes him recite, “We have gone to heaven, to the gods; we have become immortal, O King... for the sake of food. [He recites: “We have become immortal, we have become kings. 35. With the *ruṣaputra* [formula], “...for the sake of food,” he places it in front. 36. He recites, “We have become immortal, we have become kings.”

35. ... (7? From the east they strike with a tuft of *rūṣa* grass, saying, "For food thee!"—from the south the Brahman priest, saying, "For strength thee!"—from the west the Hotṛ priest, saying, "For the winning of strength thee!"—and from the north the Udgātṛ priest;
thus do the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the non-officiating priests strike together.
Regarding this, they say: "He comes with dust. If he comes, [it is said]: "By means of sacrifice, he fashioned life" (four times).

With these [verses], including "Thou art immortality," he establishes himself upon the *śatamāna* coin; with "Thou art nourishment," upon the goat-skin; and with "Thou art procreation," upon the earth.
At this time, to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, a stool made of Udumbara wood has been prepared, covered with that very black antelope skin. The sacrificer mounts it and sits upon it,
having turned toward the east and drawn his knees together.
With the words, "For plowing thee," they take [the wooden sword]; with "For security thee," he places it in the pit to the east of the *sadas*;
with "Recite for Indra accompanied by the Maruts," he proceeds with the three *marutvatīya* offerings in the established manner.

"O King, you are the one who partakes," with these words he descends for the consumption of the *marutvatīya* cup. Following it, the *anvatigrāhya* cups are offered; five cups for Indra are offered. Their consumption is as follows: "May Indra place speech within us; may the divine drop (*indu*) place speech within us; may he bestow [strength] upon us; may wealth and sacrifices, accompanied by all-heroic sons, attend us; the honeyed, powerful consumption has been invoked. Thus the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) is completed.
The third pressing is accomplished from the Āgrayaṇa vessel;
having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he proceeds with the animal sacrifices in their respective places.
For these, there are separate *manotā* hymns, separate oblations, and separate touchings.
This is common for those [offerings] dedicated to various deities; this is entirely common for those dedicated to Prajāpati.
For these, they lead forward the *ukthas* with the formulas "the Vanaspati," "the Sviṣṭakṛt," and "the Quarters as the *iḍā*.
The *ukthas* are successfully completed; he leads forward the *ṣoḍaśin*.

The *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is thus established. Then [the Adhvaryu] says, "O *hotṛ*s, fill your goblets after [yours]. Whether the Soma is flowing or not flowing, the Adhvaryu says, "O Unnetṛ, do not let the Soma overflow, as if it were water. Having offered the final *sāvitra* oblation with four spoonfuls (*caturgṛhīta*), and having offered the names [of the deities] within the vow (*vrata*), he recites: "I have proclaimed thy names, O Śipiviṣṭa."

Having touched water, he touches the house with the mantra: "Today, O fair-cheeked one, on this auspicious day of the days, drink the Soma, being in great harmony; O Viṣṇu, stride across the three worlds! Having taken the *prastara* grass-bundle, he hastens away with the chant;
the *chandomas* sing the final *bṛhat* hymn, and he responds to them. Having said, "This is the redundant *uktha*; let it go to Indra through speech," he hastens away.

Having said, "Come, O sacrificer," the Adhvaryu enters the two *havirdhāna* sheds and pours these cups into ten-by-ten sets of *camasa*s. Having taken hold of the *hotṛcamasa* following the *saptahotṛcamasa*, he causes the announcement to be made;
he says, "O, announce!"—"Let the reciter of the *uktha* sacrifice to Soma.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, they offer; when the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, they offer.

With the oblation of the Hotṛ, he offers; they come and consume [it], saying: "This honeyed portion for the gods, O Viṣṇu, which you drank when you strode out across the worlds in three steps—having drunk it, you have made wide room for us. I consume you, the pressed Soma, who are my self, my father, and the sustainer of my breaths. You are the giver of luster, the giver of body, and the giver of milk. I consume you, the pressed one, who are savory and possessed of the *śipiviṣṭa* form, for the sake of sovereign rule; I consume you as the impelled medicine."
"Born from the fire that consumes all things," they purify themselves (38).
"Impel my limbs, O Lord of the Bay Steeds," they touch themselves (39).
"O Aśvins, restore sight to my two eyes," with these words, the Āgnīdhra pours the embers of the *aupayaja* offerings onto the *dhiṣṇya* of the Hotṛ.
With twenty-two *upayaj* offerings he approaches. He throws two by two into the *upayaj* fire. With twenty-two *viṣkalī* bones they perform the *saṃyājana* for the wives.
The rite is successfully accomplished; the *Vājapeya* comes to a conclusion.
Regarding this, they say: "One who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice should not descend [to greet anyone]; for he is one who does not descend.
To this they reply: "Indeed, there is a person whom it is not possible to descend to greet—a teacher, or one initiated for a sacrifice, or a king, or a father."
For him, a circular skin, a brush, and six pairs of sandals are prepared.
With two of them he moves within the *śālā* (the sacrificial hall); with two he attends to the fires; with two he goes out into the forest.
When he is about to initiate a student, he sits down on that circular skin to the south of the *Āhavanīya* fire.
He remains bound by desire at will; having released himself from desire, he moves about in this very manner until the *pratyavarohaṇīya* sacrifice.
On either the [latter] fortnight or the former, he performs the *pratyavarohaṇīya* sacrifice.
On a chosen site for the sacrifice to the gods, they erect the hall.

For this purpose, the following items are prepared: a throne-seat made of Udumbara wood, along with a cushion and a mat. Intending to perform the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, he places the Udumbara throne-seat to the south of the Āhavanīya fire.
He places upon it a cushion and a broom; he spreads it out, and the sacrificer mounts it.
While [the Adhvaryu] holds on to him, he offers the oblation with: “From the earth, the tree; from the tree, the atmosphere; ascending upwards, ascend, svāhā! [K4,68b3]
They remove the stool; sitting on the cushion (kaśipu), he takes hold [of the ladle].

While he has taken hold, he offers [the oblation] with: "From the intermediate space I have gone to heaven; from heaven I have gone to the firmament (nāka). From the back of the firmament of heaven, I, the light of *suvar*, have ascended. Rising upwards, ascend, svāhā! They remove [the ladle]; sitting on the cushion and the grass-bundle (kūrca), he takes hold [of it].

When [the disciple] has taken hold [of him], he offers [an oblation] with: “Go forth! Come on! Be bold! Your thunderbolt shall not fail; O Indra, let your manly power be directed toward the curse; rise up, ascend, svāhā!”—thus he undergoes the consecration in the established manner.
He undergoes initiation according to the established rule;
when he uncovers himself before the King (Soma), then these two sandals are released, and he throws them upon the rubbish-heap.
The Catuṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma is already well-established;
its sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) amount to twelve hundred.
Of these, for every hundred, a man has a hundred-year lifespan and a hundredfold sensory power (*indriya*); thus he becomes firmly established in both lifespan and sensory power.
Now, as for those [days] by twelves—twelve months make a year; verily, he finds firm support in the year itself.

Regarding this, they say: "He who sacrifices with the Vājapeya indeed falls away from this world; he runs the race and ascends the sacrificial post. If he were not to sacrifice with the *pratyavarohaṇīya* (the descent-offering), he would ascend to that world beyond and be liable to perish. Furthermore, if he were not to offer these oblations, he would not return even from those worlds which he has won through the Vājapeya. Therefore, when he sacrifices with the *pratyavarohaṇīya*, he [returns] to this very world by means of it."

He stands firm in this world and does not meet with misfortune; he reaches his full span of life. Now, because he offers these oblations, he returns from that world. Of that Vājapeya which he has won, there are twelve stotras; twelve months are a year, and thus he stands firm in the year itself. It has twenty-four *stuta* and *śastra* chants; twenty-four [are the half-months].

The half-months are the year; verily he finds firm support in the year. Now, as for the fact that it is a *catuṣṭoma* *agniṣṭoma*: there are four quarters; verily he finds firm support in the quarters, verily he finds firm support in the quarters. Thus the *Vājapeya* is completed.

By this manifestation, generating mighty deeds, he indeed is the glowing one; wide is the path for the seeker. He has risen up as the supporter at the forefront of the honeyed draught, when he impelled his own body by means of his body. (1.7.12.2.g) You are taken with a base; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. This is your womb; for Prajāpati, you!

2. Surely, indeed, just as those possessing barley reap the barley, separating it in due order, so do you prepare here and there the food for those who have not come to the trimming of the sacred grass (*barhis*) with their homage.
Honeyed are the winds for the one who follows the cosmic order; honey do the rivers flow. May the plants be sweet for us.

4. Cf. BŚS 11.6:72.9. He brings it down [from the cart] with the mantra: "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; may this man slay Vṛtra with thee. 5. Cf. BŚS 11.6:72.10. Then, while it is still held by the pole, they turn it toward the interior of the sacrificial ground (antarvedi) with the mantra: "In the impulse of strength, we celebrate with our speech the great Mother named Aditi, in whom this entire world has entered; may the god Savitṛ impel for us the righteous order within her."

6. Cf. BŚS 11.6:72.13. Then he washes the horses in the waters with [the verse]: "In the waters is immortality, in the waters is healing; and in the praises of the waters, O horses, become winners of the prize.

7. Cf. BŚS 11.6:72.15. Then he yokes the right-hand horse with [the verse]: "Whether Vāyu has yoked you, or Manu, or the twenty-seven Gandharvas—they yoked the horse in the beginning; they placed speed in him."
8. Cf. BŚS (1.7.7.2.f): "O Son of the Waters, swift-impelling, that wave which is peaked, surging, and most effective in winning booty—with that may this one win booty.
Then he cleanses its back: "O Son of the Waters, swift-impelling, that wave which is peaked, surging, and most effective in winning booty—with that may this one win booty.
9. Cf. BŚS (11.7:75.6): Then he approaches the chariot: "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu; thou art the step of Viṣṇu; thou art the wide-stride of Viṣṇu."
10. Then he touches the two sides of the chariot with the mantra: "The two hooks, the two side-hooks, which are on both sides of the chariot.
11. He mounts the chariot with the mantra: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I win the prize through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize.
12. At this time, the Brahman ascends the marked chariot wheel.

For this very reason, he addresses him with the mantra: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I ascend the highest firmament through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize. [TS 1.7.8.1b] Then, having caused the sacrificer to sit down behind him, he makes him recite seventeen *ujjitīḥ* (victories), beginning with: "Agni won speech by means of the one-syllable [meter]. [TS 1.7.11]
Then he hands him a horse-whip with [the verse]: "O horse-whip, powerful one, full of power in contests for booty, make the horses swift in battles!
With that, he strikes the horses as is appropriate. [With the formula:
"Thou art a courser," he strikes the right [horse].
With the words, "Thou art a steed, *m*," he addresses the middle one; with the words, "Thou art a prize-winner, *m*," the upper one.
He consecrates the voices that have been uttered together with the mantra: "Speak speech for Indra; cause Indra to win the prize; Indra has won the prize."
17. Cf. BŚS 11.9:78.17. As these race-horses approach him, he distributes one *kṛṣṇala* to each of them.

18. Cf. BŚS 11.7:75.4. He causes these horses, yoked by the *yajus*, to smell [the offering] with the mantra: "O prize-winning steeds, about to run for the prize and about to win the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati! (TS 1.7.8.o).

19. *Mantra* var.? Cf. ṚV 1.7.8.1.e: "Thou art swift; thou art a steed; thou art a prize-winner. 20. Cf. VŚS 11.8:77.1: When the *sāman* has been introduced, he issues the command: "O *Brahman*, [drive] the prize-winners! O singers, run the race! Beat the drums! Pressers, press! *Āgnīdh*, pour out the milk-mixture! Make the mortar resound! *Pratiprasthātṛ*, offer the cake on one potsherd for Varuṇa; take note of the offering for Soma!"
21. O prize-winners, run for the prize; conquer in the impulse of the Maruts; measure out the distances;

steady the paths; reach the goal! 22. In every contest for the prize, O prize-winners, protect us; you who are wise, immortal, and knowers of the Truth (*ṛta*). Drink of this honeyed mead; rejoice; being satisfied, go by the paths traveled by the gods.

(1.7.8.2) May all those swift steeds, who hear our invocation, hear our call— (1.7.8.2.i) The well-paced runners, winners of a thousandfold, eager for gain in the winning of the prize; they who have displayed great valor in the battles—may the swift steeds be auspicious to us at our invocations. (1.7.8.2.k) At the assembly of the gods, may the well-paced, well-praising ones, crushing the serpent, the wolf, and the demons, drive them away from us entirely— (1.7.8.3) [And] all maladies.

(1.7.8.3ḷ) This vigorous steed hastens toward the whip, bound by the neck, the flanks, and the mouth; Dadhikrā, exerting his strength in accordance with his will, springs along the curves of the paths.
23. Cf. *BŚS* (11.8:78.3): "The chariots come; having seen the chariots that have arrived, he asks for a vessel of clarified butter together with a *sruva*-ladle.

If they report to him a mishap involving the chariot, the *Āgnīdhra* offers this [oblation] with both [verses]: 'And indeed, of him as he runs, as he hastens... etc. (TS 1.7.8.m). Thus, by means of both [verses].

And indeed, as he runs and hastens forward, eager for the prize, the wind blows after him like the wing of a bird; as Dadhikrāvan speeds along with his might, he passes by the bend like a swooping falcon.

May the impulse of strength come to me; may Heaven and Earth, the source of all well-being, come to me; may my two fathers and my two mothers come to me; may Soma come to me for the sake of immortality.
Cf. BŚS 11.8:78.6: He offers the *rathavimocanīya* oblation with the verse: "May the impulse of strength come to me. (TS 1.7.8ṇ).

26. Cf. BŚS 11.9:78.11. He causes these horses, yoked by the *yajus*, to smell [the offering] with the mantra: "O prize-winning, prize-conquering horses, having run for the prize and having won the prize, wipe yourselves in the portion of Bṛhaspati.
27. Cf. BŚS 11.7:75.12. Then, having mounted behind the sacrificer, he makes him recite the *ujjitīs*: "Agni won speech with the one-syllable [meter]," and so on, seventeen [verses].

28. Having caused [the sacrificer] to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, he causes the sacrificer to approach the *soma*-cups with the formula: "You are united; unite me with prosperity. He approaches the *surā*-cups with the formula: "You are separated; separate me from evil."

29. "You are separators; separate me from evil," [with these words] he offers the cups of *surā*. Then, taking this *surā* together with the residue and these cups of *surā*, they present them to the race-runners (*ājisṛt*).

30. With a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, he makes an offering for each [portion] and performs seven oblations of food, [reciting]: "The impulse of strength has impelled this in the beginning. 31. "O wife, come! Let us two ascend to heaven; indeed, let us two ascend to heaven. I shall cause both of us to ascend to heaven."

Cf. BŚS 11.11:80.2; TS 1.7.9.b: "Then he addresses his wife: 'Wife, come! Let us two ascend to heaven! She replies: 'Let us two indeed ascend to heaven! The sacrificer says: 'I shall cause both of us to ascend to heaven! The wife says: 'May you cause both of us to ascend to heaven! [Then: 'May life be perfected through sacrifice; may breath be perfected through sacrifice; may the out-breath..."

32. Cf. *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* (1.7.9.1ḍ): "May life be perfected through sacrifice; may out-breath be perfected through sacrifice; may in-breath be perfected through sacrifice; may diffused breath be perfected through sacrifice; may sight be perfected through sacrifice; may hearing be perfected through sacrifice; may mind be perfected through sacrifice; may speech be perfected through sacrifice; may the self be perfected through sacrifice;
may sacrifice itself be perfected through sacrifice. Cf. *Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra* (11.11:80.5): "He ascends it with ten perfections, [beginning] with 'May life be perfected through sacrifice.'"

Having offered the twelve Vājaprasavīya oblations with the formulas beginning "Vāja and Prasava," the sacrificer ascends the sacrificial post by means of the ladder with the ten *kalpa* formulas beginning "May life be perfected through the sacrifice."

33. *Haṃsaḥ śuciṣad vasur antarikṣasad dhotā vediṣad atithir duroṇasat | nṛṣad varasad ṛtasad vyomasad abjā gojā ṛtajā adrijā ṛtaṃ bṛhat* // Having offered the oblations for unyoking the chariot (*rathavimocanīya*) with the formula, "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā," he places the chariot upon the chariot-stand together with the charioteer, reciting: "*Haṃsaḥ śuciṣad...* 34.
*Suvar devān aganmāmṛtā abhūma prajāpateḥ prajā abhūma* // (We have gone to the light of heaven, we have become immortal; we have become the offspring of Prajāpati.)
Having gone to the end, he raises his arms, saying: "O gods, we have gone to heaven; we have become immortal; O Prajāpati, we have become your offspring.
Then they strike him with handfuls of grass.

"Thou art for food," says the Adhvaryu from the east; "thou art for the eating of food," says the Brahman from the south; "thou art for strength," says the Hotṛ from the west; "thou art for the winning of strength," says the Udgātṛ from the north.
"Thou art immortality, thou art nourishment, thou art procreation."

37. [Mantra fragment] ... May Indra bestow power (*indriya*) upon us; may wealth and sacrifices attend us; may blessings be with us. May she be dear to us—she who is victorious, the bountiful one. 38. [Cf. Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.2.5.3ḷ] Impel my limbs, O Lord of the Bay Steeds (*harivas*); let not my vital groups thirst for you. Be auspicious to me as you approach the Seven Seers (*saptarṣis*); do not pass over my navel. (3.2.5.4) Do not go beyond!
Agni has given sight back; Indra and Bṛhaspati have given it back. O Aśvins, you two restore sight to my eyes.
For a year he should not descend toward anyone at all; for these two do not descend toward anyone at all—this is their vow.
